chooseSection.heading: How to Choose a Bluevine Alternative
chooseSection.body:
Selecting a Bluevine alternative requires matching your operating cash patterns against published monthly fees, deposit yields, transaction costs and borrowing terms. Bluevine provides high-yield business checking alongside an embedded revolving credit facility. Evaluating replacements depends on six primary operational criteria.

First, calculate the monthly account cost. Bluevine Standard, Mercury, Relay Starter and Novo charge $0 in monthly service fees with no minimum balance rules. Lili Core charges $0, while its Pro, Smart and Premium accounts charge monthly fees whose exact amounts are not published on the checked pages. In contrast, Chase Business Complete Banking charges $15 per month ($180 per year) unless the fee is avoided, while Chase Performance costs $40 per month ($480 per year) and Chase Platinum costs $95 per month ($1,140 per year). 

Second, evaluate interest rates and yields on idle balances. Bluevine Standard yields 1.3% APY on balances up to $250,000 when spending $500 monthly on the debit card or depositing $2,500 monthly in customer receipts. Bluevine Plus pays 1.75% APY up to $250,000 for $30 per month, and Premier pays 3.3% APY on all balances for $95 per month. Among alternatives, Relay pays 1.19% APY on savings in Starter, 1.87% APY in Grow ($30 per month), and 3.21% APY in Scale ($90 per month). Lili pays 2.25% APY on savings balances up to $500,000 and 4.00% APY on balances from $500,000 up to $1,000,000 across all tiers. Novo Savings pays 2% APY at balances of $50,000 or more. Mercury provides a Treasury account for balances of $250,000 or more, while Chase business checking accounts do not advertise base interest yields.

Third, verify FDIC insurance coverage limits. Standard FDIC insurance protects up to $250,000 per depositor per institution. Bluevine, Relay and Lili extend FDIC protection up to $3,000,000 by distributing funds across partner sweep networks. Mercury and Novo provide sweep coverage protecting deposits up to $5,000,000. 

Fourth, assess transaction charges and physical branch access. Bluevine includes free incoming domestic wires and free standard ACH payments, but applies charges for outgoing wires and international payments. Mercury provides free incoming and outgoing ACH transfers, domestic wires, international wires and real-time payments across all plans. Chase provides physical branch teller transactions and fee-free cash deposits up to $5,000 per cycle on Business Complete Banking, but restricts fee-free wire allowances to higher-tier checking accounts. 

Fifth, review credit availability. Bluevine offers an embedded business line of credit up to $250,000 with no monthly maintenance fees and automatic weekly or monthly repayments. Lili embeds flexible capital up to $250,000. OnDeck operates as a dedicated commercial financing lender, providing revolving lines of credit from $6,000 to $200,000 with an average published rate of 59.8% Annual Percentage Rate (APR), and term loans up to $400,000 with an average rate of 53.2% APR. Mercury, Relay and Novo do not list a line of credit on their pricing pages, though Novo offers a business credit card with up to 2% cash back and Relay offers credit cards with cash back scaling from 1% to 1.5%.

Sixth, check business formation and entity restrictions. Bluevine requires a business to be structured as a corporation or Limited Liability Company (LLC) to qualify for its line of credit, excluding sole proprietorships from borrowing. OnDeck requires an operational business checking account, one year in business, and $100,000 in annual revenue. Lili limits international wire transfers exclusively to LLCs, corporations and partnerships.

Who This Is Not For:

- Companies in Nevada, North Dakota, South Dakota, or United States territories, which cannot obtain a Bluevine Line of Credit.
- Sole proprietors, because the Bluevine Line of Credit requires an LLC or corporation.
- Businesses that need branch cash deposits beyond what Chase offers.
- Personal finance readers, because this page covers business accounts only.

What Would Change Our Answer:

- Bluevine altering its 1.3%, 1.75% or 3.3% checking APY rates or removing its debit spend and deposit activity requirements on Standard.
- Relay, Mercury or Novo introducing an integrated revolving commercial line of credit to rival Bluevine.
- Chase removing its $15 monthly fee on Business Complete Banking or eliminating branch deposit allowances.
- OnDeck lowering its $100,000 revenue qualification minimum or publishing individual risk-tier rates below its 53.2% and 59.8% APR averages.
- Lili publishing specific monthly plan prices for its Pro, Smart and Premium accounts.

alternatives.heading: Mercury Banking Plans and Fee Structure
alternatives.body:
Mercury is a financial technology company, not a bank, providing banking services and essential tools. Its base Mercury plan costs $0 per month with no monthly service charges, no overdraft penalties, and no minimum balance requirements. Deposits are FDIC-insured up to $5,000,000 through partner sweep banks. Mercury provides free domestic and international wire transfers, free ACH payments, and free real-time payments on its entry plan.

Mercury Plus costs $29.90 per month on annual billing (a 15% discount) and includes a 30-day free trial. Mercury Plus adds invoice processing with ACH debits at $1 per transaction, recurring billing tools, unlimited 1099 tax filings, priority customer support. Six months of free Xero accounting software. Mercury Pro costs $299 per month on annual billing, providing a dedicated relationship manager, $0 transaction fees on invoice ACH debits, and custom NetSuite transaction categorizations. Optional add-ons include Mercury Books at $35 per month and Mercury Payroll at $100 per month plus $50 per person paid, with both add-on fees waived through December 31, 2026. Mercury Treasury unlocks for accounts holding at least $250,000, and Mercury Personal accounts are free for business plan holders.

Over twelve months, base Mercury costs $0 in account maintenance fees, Mercury Plus costs $358.80 ($29.90 x 12), and Mercury Pro costs $3,588 ($299 x 12). If an enterprise sends ten domestic and five international wires each month, Mercury charges $0 across all fifteen transfers. On Bluevine, outgoing wire transfers incur transaction fees.

Mercury fits businesses that require high FDIC sweep coverage up to $5,000,000 and frequent wire transfers with zero transaction fees. Versus Bluevine, Mercury falls short on embedded credit, as its fee schedule does not list an integrated business line of credit. Mercury also lacks native interest on base checking balances below the $250,000 Treasury minimum.

alternatives.heading: Relay Checking Tiers and Multi-Account Features
alternatives.body:
Relay provides business banking accounts through Thread Bank, Member FDIC, offering deposit protection up to $3,000,000 through sweep networks. Relay enforces no minimum balance requirements and charges no hidden fees or overdraft penalties. All accounts include invoice generation, payment tracking, unlimited user seats, and accounting integrations.

Relay Starter costs $0 per month and provides 20 individual checking accounts, built-in employee spending controls, 1.19% APY on linked savings balances, and a business credit card earning 1% cash back. Relay Grow costs $30 per month ($360 annually) following a 14-day free trial, offering 1.87% APY on savings, 1.25% credit card cash back, multi-step approval workflows, recurring invoicing, and automated bookkeeping rules. Relay Scale lists a promotional price of $90 per month ($1,080 annually), marked down from its regular $120 monthly price ($1,440 annually). Relay Scale provides 50 checking accounts per business entity, 3.21% APY on savings, 1.5% credit card cash back, and zero-fee same-day ACH transfers. Additional transaction charges apply as disclosed on Relay's pricing page.

A business maintaining a $100,000 savings balance in Relay Scale earns $3,210 annually at 3.21% APY. Subtracting the $1,080 promotional annual plan fee leaves $2,130 in net interest. On Relay Starter, that same $100,000 balance earns $1,190 in annual interest at 1.19% APY with $0 in maintenance fees. By comparison, Bluevine Premier yields 3.3% APY on all checking balances ($3,300 on $100,000), which nets $2,160 after subtracting its $1,140 annual plan fee ($95 x 12).

Relay fits businesses managing multiple operating cash reserves across up to 50 checking accounts with multi-user approval hierarchies. Versus Bluevine, Relay falls short on embedded financing, as it does not provide an integrated business line of credit up to $250,000. Relay also requires users to move funds into designated savings accounts to earn interest, whereas Bluevine pays interest directly on checking balances.

alternatives.heading: Novo No-Fee Business Checking and Reserves
alternatives.body:
Novo provides business checking accounts, reporting over 250,000 independent business customers. Account opening takes approximately ten minutes online. Novo charges $0.00 in monthly maintenance fees and enforces a $0.00 minimum balance rule. Customer deposits are protected by FDIC sweep insurance up to $5,000,000.

Novo includes free invoicing tools, integrated payroll reserves, and free business tax filing for qualifying organizations. Novo allows customers to allocate money into reserve envelopes, including a Taxes reserve for setting money aside. Novo Savings pays 2% APY once the balance reaches $50,000, and Novo checking earns no interest. Novo also provides the Novo Business Credit Card, which features no annual fee and delivers up to 2% cash back on eligible business purchases.

A company operating on Novo pays $0 in annual software and maintenance costs ($0.00 x 12). A $25,000 balance on Novo earns $0 in interest, because the 2% APY starts at $50,000, where it would earn $1,000 per year. That same $25,000 balance in Bluevine Standard yields 1.3% APY, producing $325 annually, provided the account meets the $500 monthly debit spend or $2,500 deposit requirement.

Novo fits businesses that want fee-free checking, reserve envelopes and cash back cards. Versus Bluevine, Novo falls short on credit depth. Novo does not provide an integrated commercial line of credit comparable to Bluevine's $250,000 Celtic Bank facility.

alternatives.heading: Lili Core Checking and Tiered Savings Interest
alternatives.body:
Lili is a financial technology company, not a bank, offering commercial banking services through Sunrise Banks, N.A., Member FDIC. Lili reports serving more than 200,000 businesses and provides FDIC insurance up to $3,000,000 across its program sweep network. Lili provides express ACH transfers, domestic wires, and international wire transfers, with international wire functionality reserved strictly for LLCs, general partnerships, and corporate business entities.

Lili Core costs $0 per month with no minimum balance requirements. Lili offers paid Pro, Smart, and Premium tiers that incorporate bookkeeping tools, invoicing systems, tax preparation forms, and cash back rewards; however, specific dollar subscription prices for those paid tiers are not published on the checked website pages. Lili includes an optional BusinessBuild credit-building add-on, featuring a one-month free trial, then $18 per month for three months, followed by $30 per month ($294 in the first year), with payments reported to Dun & Bradstreet. Lili provides embedded flexible business capital up to $250,000 directly inside the account. Across all account plans, Lili offers a high-yield savings account paying 2.25% APY on balances up to $500,000, and 4.00% APY on balances above $500,000 up to $1,000,000, under rates effective January 13, 2026.

A company holding a $600,000 savings balance at Lili earns 2.25% APY on the first $500,000 ($11,250) and 4.00% APY on the remaining $100,000 ($4,000), generating $15,250 in total annual interest. On Bluevine Premier, a $600,000 balance earns 3.3% APY on the entire amount ($19,800), netting $18,660 after subtracting the $1,140 annual membership fee.

Lili fits businesses seeking up to 4.00% APY on balances alongside integrated accounting and tax preparation. Versus Bluevine, Lili falls short on pricing clarity, as its public overview pages do not publish subscription costs for its Pro, Smart and Premium accounts. Lili also restricts international wire access exclusively to LLCs, corporations and partnerships.

alternatives.heading: Chase Branch Banking and Deposit Tiers
alternatives.body:
Chase notes that more small business owners choose Chase than any other commercial bank. Business accounts integrate mobile card processing to accept debit and credit card payments directly from compatible mobile devices.

Chase Business Complete Banking lists a monthly service fee of $15 or $0 depending on whether the fee is avoided. The account includes up to 20 paper and teller-assisted transactions and up to $5,000 in monthly in-branch cash deposits per statement cycle. Chase Performance Business Checking charges a monthly service fee of $40 or $0, covering up to 250 account debits, $20,000 in monthly cash deposits, all incoming wire transfers, and the two most expensive domestic outgoing wire fees per statement cycle. Chase Platinum Business Checking carries a monthly fee of $95 or $0, providing 500 account debits, $25,000 in cash deposits, all incoming wires, and the four most expensive outgoing wire transfers per cycle. Chase waives business savings account fees when linked to a qualifying business checking account.

A business on Chase Business Complete Banking that does not avoid the monthly fee pays $180 per year ($15 x 12). On Chase Performance, the annual fee is $480 ($40 x 12). On Chase Platinum, the annual fee is $1,140 ($95 x 12). If a business deposits $4,000 in physical cash each month, Chase processes the cash for $0 in extra charges on Business Complete Banking. 

Chase fits business owners handling routine physical cash deposits who need branch and ATM access. Versus Bluevine, Chase falls short on base checking interest, as Chase Business Complete Banking does not pay high-yield interest on operational checking balances. Chase Business Complete Banking includes up to 20 paper and teller transactions per statement cycle.

alternatives.heading: OnDeck Business Lines of Credit and Term Loans
alternatives.body:
OnDeck is an online commercial lender focused on short-term business financing, having funded over 185,000 businesses and delivered more than $25 billion in capital since 2006. OnDeck does not offer business checking accounts, operating solely as a financing alternative for companies seeking lines of credit or term loans. Loan contracts are originated by Celtic Bank or entities within the OnDeck family of companies.

OnDeck provides commercial lines of credit ranging from $6,000 to $200,000 with repayment periods of 12, 18, or 24 months. Borrowers must make an initial minimum draw of $1,000. Based on loans originated in the six-month period ending June 30, 2026, OnDeck reports an average line-of-credit interest rate of 59.8% APR, with lower rates limited to applicants with the strongest credit profiles. OnDeck also issues fixed-term business loans from $5,000 to $400,000 with terms up to 24 months, carrying a published average rate of 53.2% APR. Checking eligibility requires no hard credit pull, and approved loans can disburse capital as fast as the same business day. OnDeck charges origination fees, late fees, and returned payment fees, with 0% origination fees reserved for qualifying renewal borrowers.

Qualification standards require at least one year in business, an active business checking account, a minimum personal Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) score of 625, and at least $100,000 in verifiable annual gross revenue. On a $50,000 line of credit maintained for a full year at OnDeck's 59.8% average APR, the annual interest calculation equals $29,900 ($50,000 x 0.598), assuming the balance remains constant without principal reduction. Bluevine's line-of-credit interest rates vary according to creditworthiness and are not itemized as a single average on its checked overview pages.

OnDeck fits companies that need fast secondary borrowing up to $200,000 without switching their current primary checking account. Versus Bluevine, OnDeck falls short on borrowing limits and overall banking integration. Bluevine offers revolving lines up to $250,000 (compared to OnDeck's $200,000 cap) and integrates borrowing directly into high-yield checking, with instant draws into a Bluevine account and zero monthly line maintenance fees.

stillBetterFit.heading: When Bluevine Is Still the Better Fit
stillBetterFit.body:
Bluevine remains the closer match for incorporated small businesses that want high-yield operational checking paired with fast revolving credit. Bluevine Standard provides 1.3% APY on checking balances up to $250,000 for $0 per month when spending $500 monthly on the debit card or depositing $2,500 monthly. Companies seeking higher yields can choose Bluevine Plus (1.75% APY up to $250,000 for $30 per month) or Bluevine Premier (3.3% APY on all balances for $95 per month), with monthly plan fees waivable upon meeting specified criteria.

Bluevine also provides an embedded business line of credit up to $250,000 with no ongoing maintenance fees, credit decisions in as fast as five minutes. Instant draws directly into Bluevine Business Checking. Borrowers can choose weekly or monthly automatic repayment schedules, and account performance reports to Experian. Bluevine checking includes up to 50 dedicated sub-accounts with custom transfer rules, bill payment tools, invoicing, estimates, and payment links. Solo business owners can compare billing tools in our [freelance invoicing apps roundup](/roundup/best-invoicing-apps-for-freelancers/) or review loan requirements in our [small business financing guide](/guides/small-business-financing-guide/).

Businesses structured as an LLC or corporation with at least $10,000 in monthly revenue, 12 months of operating history. A 625+ personal FICO score get an operational checking account and credit line without paying separate platform fees.

verdict: Bluevine pairs high-yield checking with an embedded business line of credit up to $250,000. Mercury, Relay and Novo offer $0 monthly checking plans with specialized sweep features, Lili provides tiered savings interest, with 4.00% APY only from $500,000, Chase delivers widespread branch and cash deposit access, and OnDeck offers dedicated commercial credit up to $200,000. Next step: total your monthly cash deposits and borrowing needs, then read our [business line of credit requirements guide](/guides/business-line-of-credit-requirements/) alongside the table above.

faqs.question: Is Bluevine a bank?
faqs.answer: No. Bluevine is a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services and FDIC insurance coverage up to $3,000,000 are provided through Coastal Community Bank, Member FDIC, and its program banks.

faqs.question: Does Bluevine charge monthly fees?
faqs.answer: Bluevine Standard charges no monthly service fees and has no minimum balance requirement. Bluevine Plus costs $30 per month and Bluevine Premier costs $95 per month, though Bluevine states both monthly fees can be waived upon meeting specific activity conditions.

faqs.question: What is the Bluevine line of credit minimum revenue?
faqs.answer: Bluevine requires at least $10,000 in monthly revenue, which equals $120,000 in annual revenue. Applicants must also operate as an LLC or corporation for at least 12 months, hold a personal FICO score of 625 or higher, and have no bankruptcies on file.

faqs.question: Which Bluevine alternative has no monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Mercury, Relay Starter, Novo, and Lili Core all offer business checking accounts with $0 monthly maintenance fees and no minimum balance requirements.

faqs.question: Does Bluevine pay interest on checking?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bluevine Standard pays 1.3% APY on balances up to $250,000 if you spend $500 per month on the debit card or deposit $2,500 per month. Bluevine Plus pays 1.75% APY up to $250,000 with no requirements, and Bluevine Premier pays 3.3% APY on all balances.

title: Empower Alternatives 2026: Pricing and Features Compared
h1: Empower Alternatives 2026: Pricing and Features Compared
metaDescription: Empower alternatives compared: Monarch Money, YNAB, Quicken Simplifi, Betterment, Wealthfront and Fidelity Go, with published prices and advisory fees.
intro:
The primary alternatives to Empower are Monarch Money, YNAB, Quicken Simplifi, Betterment, Wealthfront and Fidelity Go. We show the fee arithmetic so you can see whether a free dashboard, a paid budgeting subscription or an automated investment advisory account fits your goals.

[Empower](https://www.empower.com/) divides its platform into two parts: free personal wealth tools and paid wealth management. The free tools cover net worth tracking, a retirement planner, portfolio analysis and budgeting. Its paid wealth management begins at $100,000 for Personal Strategy and $1,000,000 for Private Client, with advisory fees calculated on assets managed as disclosed in its Form ADV rather than published as a flat rate on its public pages. For cash, Empower Personal Cash offers a 3.50% Annual Percentage Yield (APY) with up to $5 million in Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) coverage.

Because Empower combines investment management with financial tracking, your choice depends on whether you need budgeting software or an investment manager. For deeper breakdowns in each category, see our [Monarch Money alternatives](/alternatives/monarch-money/) comparison, our [YNAB alternatives](/alternatives/ynab/) guide, our [Wealthfront alternatives](/alternatives/wealthfront/) review, our [Quicken alternatives](/alternatives/quicken/) overview, and our [financial product comparison hub](/compare/).

Empower Personal Cash lists 3.50% APY (3.70% APY for Private Client)

chooseSection.heading: How to Choose an Empower Alternative
chooseSection.body:
Start by identifying the primary job you want the software to do. Empower pairs free tracking tools with a wealth management advisory service. If your goal is tracking spending, cash flow, or investments, applications such as Monarch Money, YNAB and Quicken Simplifi provide specialized software. If your goal is to have someone manage your investments, automated investment managers like Betterment, Wealthfront and Fidelity Go manage portfolios for a stated fee.

Next, evaluate how each service charges for its tools. Empower provides its digital dashboard tools at no cost, including Net Worth, Budgeting & Cash Flow, Retirement Planner, Portfolio Analysis, Savings Planner, Debt Paydown, Emergency Fund and Transactions. Empower states advisory fees for its wealth management services are calculated based on assets managed. In contrast, Monarch Money charges $99.99 per year for Core or $199.99 for Plus, YNAB charges $109 per year, and Quicken Simplifi charges $3.99 per month billed annually ($47.88 per year) or a listed $6.99 per month ($83.88 per year). When choosing tracking tools, decide whether you prefer a free dashboard or a paid subscription.

For investment advisory services, compare balance minimums and fee structures. Empower requires $100,000 for its Personal Strategy tier. That tier provides a dedicated financial advisor, custom portfolio construction, and tax optimization. Private Client requires $1,000,000. Below $100,000, Empower wealth management is not available. Betterment charges $5 a month, or 0.25% annually with $24,000 or $200 monthly deposits. Its Premium tier needs $100,000 and costs 0.65% annually. Wealthfront charges 0.25% a year. Fidelity Go charges a $0 advisory fee for accounts under $25,000, and 0.35% annually for accounts of $25,000 or more with one-on-one coaching included.

Review the cash management terms if cash yield matters to you. Empower Personal Cash provides a standard 3.50% APY with up to $5 million in aggregate FDIC insurance and no minimums or account fees, with a 3.70% APY available for eligible Private Client members. Betterment Cash Reserve lists a base 3.50% APY. A 0.75% boost applies to new clients with qualifying deposits up to $1,000,000. Joint FDIC insurance reaches $8 million.

Use this checklist to narrow your choice:

- Do you need software to track your spending and net worth, or do you need an investment manager to handle trades?
- Do you meet Empower's $100,000 minimum for Personal Strategy, or do you prefer an advisory service with lower thresholds?
- Would you rather pay an annual subscription for an ad-free budgeting app, or use Empower's free dashboard?
- Do you require direct access to a human financial advisor, or does automated portfolio rebalancing meet your requirements?
- What interest rate does your uninvested cash earn, and what is the applicable FDIC coverage limit?

alternatives.heading: Monarch Money Pricing and Tracking Features Compared with Empower
alternatives.body:
Monarch Money is a personal finance app with two subscription tiers: Core at $99.99 per year or $14.99 per month, and Plus at $199.99 per year. A promotional code offers new users 30% off the Core annual plan for the first year. The service includes a money-back guarantee. Monarch Money states that its platform is subscription-based and ad-free. The Plus tier adds forward-looking forecasting tools, tracking for multiple income sources, and deeper investment tracking.

Versus Empower, Monarch Money does not offer investment advisory services, managed accounts, or human financial planners. While Empower is an investment adviser registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) managing custom portfolios, Monarch Money provides tracking software only. Empower provides its net worth and retirement tracking dashboard at no subscription cost, whereas Monarch Money requires a paid subscription.

Worked cost example: Over one year, Monarch Money Core costs $99.99 on annual billing, or $179.88 if paid monthly at $14.99 per month. Over five years on annual billing, Monarch Money Core costs $499.95. Empower's dashboard tools cost $0 for tracking net worth, portfolio holdings, and cash flow across that same five-year period.

alternatives.heading: YNAB Budgeting Method and Pricing Compared with Empower
alternatives.body:
YNAB is a personal budgeting application. It costs $14.99 per month or $109 per year, which equates to $9.08 per month on an annual schedule. YNAB provides a 34-day free trial. Its bank synchronization supports select financial institutions across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.

YNAB fits people who want a dedicated budgeting tool with bank import.

Versus Empower, YNAB is a budgeting application, while Empower's free dashboard pairs budgeting with Net Worth, Portfolio Analysis and Retirement Planner tools. YNAB charges $109 annually for its budgeting tools.

Worked cost example: A user on YNAB pays $109 per year on the annual plan, which equals $327 over three years. Over three years, Empower charges $0 for its personal budgeting and cash flow tracking dashboard. If a user only needs budgeting and net worth tracking, Empower provides that functionality without the $109 annual subscription fee.

alternatives.heading: Quicken Simplifi Cash Flow and Tracking Versus Empower
alternatives.body:
Quicken Simplifi is a web and mobile personal finance application that monitors spending and investments. Its pricing page shows $3.99 per month billed annually alongside a listed $6.99 per month price. The platform includes a customizable Spending Plan, 12-month projected cash flow modeling, savings goals, watchlist categories, investment tracking, and net worth tracking.

Quicken Simplifi fits budgeters who want detailed forward-looking cash flow projections, category watchlists. Net worth tracking on web and mobile.

Versus Empower, Quicken Simplifi is a paid tracking tool rather than an investment advisory platform. Quicken Simplifi displays your investment holdings and performance. It does not manage portfolios, rebalance assets, or provide access to financial advisors. Empower provides its investment analysis, retirement projection, and net worth tracking tools for free. Charging for wealth management only when clients enroll in Personal Strategy or Private Client.

Worked cost example: At $3.99 per month billed annually, Quicken Simplifi costs $47.88 per year. At the listed $6.99 per month price, it costs $83.88 over 12 months, which totals $251.64 over three years. Empower provides its Net Worth, Budgeting & Cash Flow, and Retirement Planner tools for $0 across those same three years.

alternatives.heading: Betterment Advisory Fees and Cash Reserve Versus Empower
alternatives.body:
Betterment provides automated investing portfolios, human advisor access, and a high-yield cash account. For automated investing, Betterment charges a $5 monthly base fee, which drops to an annual fee of 0.25% when clients maintain a balance of at least $24,000 or set up recurring monthly deposits of $200 or more. Betterment Premium charges an annual advisory fee of 0.65% (a 0.25% digital base fee plus a 0.40% Premium fee) for accounts with at least $100,000, providing access to financial experts. Above $1,000,000 the fee steps down to 0.15% on the portion between $1 million and $2 million. Assets above $2 million pay 0.10%. Betterment Cash Reserve pays a 3.50% base APY as of September 21, 2026. New clients with qualifying deposits up to $1,000,000 get a 0.75% boost, for 4.25% APY in total. Joint FDIC insurance reaches $8 million. Betterment also supports Individual Retirement Account (IRA) transfers.

Betterment fits investors who want automated portfolio management with published percentage pricing, as well as those with $100,000 who want access to financial advisors.

Versus Empower, Betterment publishes its advisory fees directly on its website, while Empower states that fees are based on assets managed and discloses them in its Form ADV rather than as a public percentage on its website. Both services set a $100,000 minimum for human advisor access. Empower offers free tracking tools for non-clients, while Betterment charges $5 per month on investing accounts under $24,000 that lack recurring deposits.

Worked cost example: On a $100,000 portfolio enrolled in Betterment Premium, the 0.65% annual advisory fee costs $650 per year ($100,000 multiplied by 0.0065). On Betterment's digital tier at 0.25%, managing that same $100,000 costs $250 per year. For Empower Personal Strategy, the annual advisory fee is calculated on assets managed per its Form ADV schedule.

alternatives.heading: Wealthfront Automated Portfolios and Pricing Versus Empower
alternatives.body:
Wealthfront is an automated investment platform that charges a flat 0.25% annual advisory fee on the Wealthfront Portfolio. Wealthfront's pricing page illustrates that a $15,000 portfolio costs $3.18 per month at that rate. The advisory fee covers automated portfolio management and software-based tax-loss harvesting. Wealthfront also offers a brokerage account for stocks and Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs), along with cash and borrowing services.

Wealthfront fits investors who want automated, software-driven portfolio rebalancing and tax-loss harvesting.

Versus Empower, Wealthfront relies entirely on software algorithms rather than human financial planners to manage portfolios. Empower's Personal Strategy pairs clients with a human financial advisor backed by planning specialists for portfolios of $100,000 or more. On the other hand, Wealthfront publishes its 0.25% annual advisory fee plainly and does not require a $100,000 minimum to manage the Wealthfront Portfolio.

Worked cost example: On a $50,000 investment portfolio, Wealthfront charges 0.25% annually, which equals $125 per year ($50,000 multiplied by 0.0025). On a $100,000 portfolio, Wealthfront charges $250 per year. Empower requires $100,000 to enter Personal Strategy, where fees are calculated based on assets managed under its Form ADV.

alternatives.heading: Fidelity Go Advisory Tiers and Coaching Versus Empower
alternatives.body:
Fidelity Go is an automated robo-advisory service that charges tiered management fees based on account balance. Balances under $25,000 pay an annual advisory fee of $0. Balances of $25,000 or more pay an annual advisory fee of 0.35%, which includes one-on-one financial coaching sessions and automated tax-loss harvesting in taxable accounts. There is no minimum deposit required to open an account, and investing begins at $10. Fidelity Go charges no trading fees and supports 401(k) rollovers and IRA transfers.

Fidelity Go fits investors with balances under $25,000 seeking free portfolio management, as well as investors with $25,000 or more who want one-on-one coaching at a published 0.35% annual fee.

Versus Empower, Fidelity Go allows investors to access automated management at any balance size, whereas Empower's Personal Strategy requires $100,000 to work with an advisor. For accounts under $25,000, Fidelity Go charges a $0 advisory fee, providing managed investing that Empower does not offer at that balance level. For accounts with $25,000 or more, Fidelity Go provides financial coaching at a published 0.35% rate, whereas Empower provides dedicated advisor access beginning at $100,000 with fees detailed in its Form ADV.

Worked cost example: On a $20,000 portfolio, Fidelity Go charges $0 in advisory fees. On a $100,000 portfolio, Fidelity Go's 0.35% fee equals $350 per year ($100,000 multiplied by 0.0035) and includes one-on-one coaching sessions. At that same $100,000 level, Empower offers Personal Strategy with fees determined by assets managed.

alternatives.heading: Who This Is Not For
alternatives.body:
This page lists products and published fees. It does not fit these readers:

- People who want a human advisor with less than $100,000, because Empower's advisory tier starts at that balance.
- People who need Empower's advisory fee percentage before deciding, because it appears only in the Form ADV and not on the pages read.
- People who want one-fee budgeting-only software with no investing features.
- People who need a tax or legal opinion, which a fee comparison cannot give.

alternatives.heading: What Would Change Our Answer on Empower Alternatives
alternatives.body:
The comparison on this page reflects published terms and pricing checked on November 18, 2026. Several potential moves by these providers would change how they line up:

- If Empower publishes a standard advisory fee percentage for Personal Strategy directly on its website, readers could compare its cost against Betterment, Wealthfront and Fidelity Go without reviewing its Form ADV.
- If Empower introduces an advisory tier below its current $100,000 threshold, it would compete directly with Fidelity Go and Wealthfront for investors with smaller portfolios.
- If Betterment modifies its $5 monthly base fee on accounts under $24,000, it would change the entry-level comparison for new investors.
- If Fidelity Go alters its $25,000 threshold for free management or changes its 0.35% fee tier, the cost calculation for mid-sized portfolios would shift.
- If Monarch Money, YNAB or Quicken Simplifi adds automated portfolio management or native high-yield cash accounts, the boundary between budgeting software and investment platforms would blur.
- If Empower Personal Cash or Betterment Cash Reserve adjusts its base APY, the cash return comparison would require recalculation.

stillBetterFit.heading: When Empower Is Still the Better Fit
stillBetterFit.body:
Empower remains the stronger fit for individuals who want free tracking tools without paying a monthly or annual software subscription. Its free dashboard provides Net Worth tracking, a Retirement Planner, Budgeting & Cash Flow, Portfolio Analysis, a Savings Planner, Debt Paydown tracking, an Emergency Fund tracker, and Transaction tracking. Empower also provides a free portfolio analysis on its wealth management page with no obligation to enroll in paid advisory services.

Empower is also well suited for investors with $100,000 or more who want one-on-one guidance from a dedicated financial advisor backed by planning specialists. Its Personal Strategy provides customized portfolio management and tax optimization. For high-net-worth investors with $1,000,000 or more, its Private Client tier adds premium planning, private equity access, and legacy planning.

Additionally, Empower Personal Cash offers a cash option with no account fees, no minimum deposit requirements, direct deposit support, aggregate FDIC insurance up to $5 million, and a 3.50% standard APY (or 3.70% APY for eligible Private Client customers).

verdict: Empower provides free personal tracking tools paired with human wealth management for portfolios of $100,000 or more, with advisory fees detailed in its Form ADV. If you only want budgeting and net worth tracking, Monarch Money ($99.99 per year), YNAB ($109 per year) and Quicken Simplifi ($3.99 per month billed annually) offer dedicated software tools. If you want managed investing, Betterment (0.25% or 0.65% with advisors), Wealthfront (0.25%), and Fidelity Go ($0 under $25,000; 0.35% at $25,000 or more) provide clear, published percentage fees. Next step: compare your portfolio balance with the account minimums in the table above.

faqs.question: What should I use instead of Empower?
faqs.answer: If you want budgeting and spending tracking, Monarch Money, YNAB and Quicken Simplifi provide dedicated financial software. If you want automated investment management, Betterment, Wealthfront and Fidelity Go manage portfolios with published percentage fees starting from $0 to 0.35%.

faqs.question: Is Empower really free to use?
faqs.answer: Yes. Empower provides free personal dashboard tools, including its Net Worth tracker, Budgeting & Cash Flow, Retirement Planner, and Portfolio Analysis. It also offers a free portfolio analysis with no obligation to purchase advisory services. Empower charges fees only if you enroll in paid wealth management.

faqs.question: What is Empower's advisory fee?
faqs.answer: Empower states that its wealth management advisory fees are calculated based on the amount of assets managed, as detailed in the Empower Advisory Group, LLC Form ADV. The public overview pages checked do not publish a specific percentage fee.

faqs.question: How much money do you need to use Empower wealth management?
faqs.answer: Empower Personal Strategy requires a minimum investment of $100,000 to work one-on-one with a financial advisor backed by specialists. Its Private Client tier requires $1,000,000 or more in investments for specialized portfolio management and legacy planning.

faqs.question: Which Empower alternatives offer free investment management?
faqs.answer: Fidelity Go charges a $0 advisory fee for accounts with balances under $25,000. For accounts with $25,000 or more, Fidelity Go charges an annual advisory fee of 0.35%.

title: Dave Alternatives 2026: 6 Cash Advance Apps Compared
h1: Dave Alternatives 2026: 6 Cash Advance Apps Compared
metaDescription: Compare Dave alternatives for cash advances: MoneyLion, EarnIn, Varo, Cash App, Klover and Albert, with fees, advance limits and account rules compared.
intro:
MoneyLion, EarnIn, Varo, Cash App, Klover and Albert are six Dave alternatives that provide cash advances or earned wage access (EWA) when an expense arises before payday. The table below sets each app's published advance limits, delivery fees and account rules side by side.

[Dave](https://dave.com/) is a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services come from Coastal Community Bank, a member of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), or another partner bank, with deposits insured up to $250,000 on a pass-through basis against the failure of the holding bank. Dave offers ExtraCash advances from $25 to $500 with no credit check, no interest and no late fees, though Dave states that few members qualify for $500. Dave determines eligibility with CashAI technology evaluating 180 or more data points, including bank balance and irregular income. ExtraCash is structured as an overdraft with a fee equal to the greater of $5 or 5 percent, repayable on demand, and requires an ExtraCash overdraft deposit account alongside Dave Checking. Dave also charges a monthly membership fee of up to $5 that renews monthly, and deleting the app does not end it.

 For strategies to build stability, see our [guide to stopping living paycheck to paycheck](/guides/how-to-stop-living-paycheck-to-paycheck/) and our [emergency fund guide](/guides/how-much-emergency-fund/). To explore budgeting software, browse the [best budgeting apps roundup](/roundup/best-budgeting-apps/).

chooseSection.heading: How to Choose a Dave Alternative
chooseSection.body:
Four factors separate these apps: monthly subscription fees, transfer speeds and costs, maximum advance amounts, and account requirements.

Start with the fixed subscription cost. Dave charges up to $5 per month just to access its features, adding up to $60 per year before paying any advance fees. By contrast, MoneyLion Instacash, EarnIn and Klover let users request advances without paying a mandatory monthly subscription fee. Albert allows Instant Advances without a subscription, though its paid plans cost $19.99 to $39.99 per month ($239.88 to $479.88 annually).

Second, check the delivery pricing. Dave waives the transfer fee when sending ExtraCash to a Dave Checking account, but charges an optional 1.5% fee for transfers to an external debit card. On a $200 advance, that external fee is $3.00 on top of the overdraft fee. MoneyLion charges 7.5% capped at $14.99 for Turbo delivery to its Spend account, or 9% to an external debit card. On a $100 advance sent to an external card, MoneyLion Turbo costs $9.00, while a $200 advance costs $18.00. EarnIn charges a flat Lightning Speed fee starting at $3.99, while standard delivery is $0 across 1 to 2 business days. Standard delivery avoids speed surcharges.

Third, match the borrowing mechanism to your income structure. Dave relies on its CashAI engine to assess bank activity and income patterns. EarnIn uses earned wage access, allowing employees to access up to $1,500 per pay period based on hours already worked. Varo requires a direct deposit history to qualify for advances above its initial limit of $20 to $250, scaling up to $1,000. Cash App Borrow requires regular deposit activity, generally $300 monthly in paychecks, and operates in eligible states.

alternatives.heading: MoneyLion Instacash Advance Limits and Delivery Fees
alternatives.body:
MoneyLion is a financial technology company that provides banking services through Pathward, N.A., Member FDIC. Its Instacash service offers cash advances up to $500, which can increase up to $1,000 for users who set up qualifying recurring direct deposits into a MoneyLion Spend account. A paid MoneyLion membership can also raise the advance ceiling up to $700. Instacash charges no interest, no mandatory monthly fee and requires no credit check. MoneyLion notes a maximum disbursement limit of $100 per transfer.

Funds transferred to a MoneyLion Spend account arrive in 1 to 2 business days at no cost (marketed in some materials as 1 to 5 business days). For faster access, MoneyLion offers Turbo delivery within minutes for 7.5% of the advance amount, capped at $14.99. If a user routes an Instacash advance to an external debit card or eligible external checking account, standard delivery is unavailable, and Turbo delivery costs 9% of the advance. Turbo fees and tips are optional and do not change borrowing eligibility. Qualification requires a linked checking account at least two months old with regular income deposits and a positive balance. MoneyLion also provides Peer Boosts, allowing users to increase the limits of five friends each month.

Consider the arithmetic on a $100 cash advance. On Dave, a member pays up to $5 for monthly membership plus an ExtraCash overdraft fee of $5 (the greater of $5 or 5% of $100), totaling $10. Transferring that money to an external debit card adds 1.5%, or $1.50, bringing Dave's total to $11.50. On MoneyLion, the monthly membership fee is $0. Sending $100 to MoneyLion Spend with standard delivery costs $0. Choosing Turbo delivery to Spend costs 7.5%, or $7.50. Choosing Turbo delivery to an external card costs 9%, or $9.00. For a single $100 advance sent externally within minutes, MoneyLion costs $9.00 versus $11.50 on Dave.

MoneyLion falls short of Dave on single-withdrawal convenience, because MoneyLion caps individual disbursements at $100, requiring multiple transfers to access larger amounts. MoneyLion fits users who want advances up to $1,000 without paying a recurring monthly subscription.

alternatives.heading: EarnIn Earned Wage Access and Speed Fees
alternatives.body:
EarnIn provides earned wage access, allowing employees to draw against income they have already earned before payday. EarnIn states that its service is not a loan and charges no mandatory fees, no interest and no credit check. Limits depend on individual earnings and account verification, with its Live Pay feature providing up to $1,500 per pay period. EarnIn also provides an EarnIn Card with Live Pay, Balance Shield alerts, credit monitoring and Savings Jars.

Transfers sent through standard delivery take 1 to 2 business days and cost $0. Users who need funds immediately can choose Lightning Speed transfers, which start at $3.99 per transaction. Early Pay allows direct deposits to arrive up to 2 days sooner for a fee of $2.99. Tips are voluntary and do not affect access to wages.

Comparing EarnIn with Dave on a $200 advance highlights the structural difference. Dave charges up to $5 in monthly membership plus an ExtraCash overdraft fee of $10 (5% of $200 equals $10, which exceeds the $5 minimum). If transferred to an external card, Dave adds a 1.5% fee ($3.00), resulting in an outlay of $18.00. On EarnIn, an employee accessing $200 of earned wages pays $0 if using standard delivery. If selecting Lightning Speed at $3.99 and adding no optional tip, the cost is $3.99. That is up to $18.00 on Dave versus $3.99 on EarnIn for one $200 advance delivered to an external account within minutes, a gap of up to $14.01.

EarnIn fits hourly and salaried employees who want low-cost access to their accrued pay.

alternatives.heading: Varo Advance Limits and Chartered Bank Accounts
alternatives.body:
Varo Bank, N.A. is a chartered bank. Deposits are FDIC-insured up to $250,000. Unlike financial technology platforms that partner with third-party institutions, Varo holds its own banking charter. Varo's initial advance limits range from $20 to $250, and they can rise to $1,000 over time for customers who maintain qualifying direct deposit activity. Varo reports an average advance of $195. Varo charges no interest. It does charge flat fees from $1.60 to $100, depending on the advance amount.

For larger financing needs, Varo offers a Personal Line of Credit from $600 to $2,000, with an average loan size of $825, subject to qualification including account deposits. The account has no overdraft fees. It also has no minimum balance fees and no in-network automated teller machine (ATM) fees. It supports early paychecks up to 2 days ahead through direct deposit and fee-free cash deposits at over 7,500 CVS locations. Varo also offers the Believe Visa credit builder card and high-yield savings earning up to 3.75% annual percentage yield (APY) on balances up to $5,000, with 1.00% APY on higher balances. Varo requires $800 or more in monthly qualifying direct deposits and a positive balance for the 3.75% rate, which Varo lists as of October 5, 2026.

Examining the cost of an advance alongside account returns clarifies the trade-off. Borrowing $195 on Varo incurs a flat fee, while borrowing $200 on Dave costs an overdraft fee of $10 plus up to $5 for membership. On the savings side, a $5,000 balance in a Varo savings account at 3.75% APY yields $187.50 in annual interest when the deposit and balance conditions are met. Dave offers a Goals savings feature and Round Up savings, but does not publish a comparable chartered bank savings APY.

Varo falls short of Dave for people who want CashAI to evaluate an advance without a direct deposit history. Varo fits households seeking an all-in-one chartered bank account with built-in advance tiers and high savings yields.

alternatives.heading: Cash App Borrow Features and Cash Card Benefits
alternatives.body:
Cash App offers short-term loans through Cash App Borrow, issued and serviced by Square Financial Services, Inc. Borrow allows eligible users to take out loans up to $500 with no credit check. First-time borrowers have limits up to $400, and Cash App reported an average limit of $153 for spend-active first-time borrowers as of October 1, 2025. Borrow requires a $20 minimum loan and charges a flat fee disclosed inside the app before acceptance. Users typically gain eligibility by depositing $300 or more in monthly paychecks or linking an external account receiving $500 or more in monthly deposits. Borrow is not offered in Colorado, Iowa or Oregon.

Cash App also provides the Cash App Card with no monthly fees, early direct deposits up to 2 days ahead, and free overdraft coverage up to $200. Users who qualify for Cash App Green, earned by completing $500 in monthly purchases or $300 in monthly deposits, receive savings interest up to 3.5% and free ATM withdrawals across 40,000 in-network locations. Afterpay is built in for pay-over-time purchases.

Comparing loan structures illustrates the fee model. On Dave, borrowing $100 costs an overdraft fee of $5 plus the monthly membership fee of up to $5. On Cash App, users pay a flat fee disclosed at the time of the transaction, with no monthly membership charge. A user depositing $300 monthly in paychecks avoids recurring account costs on Cash App.

Cash App falls short of Dave on geographic availability, as Cash App Borrow excludes three states entirely. Dave also permits advances up to $500 based on CashAI analysis of bank transactions without requiring a direct deposit of $300. Cash App fits existing ecosystem users who already direct deposit funds and want borrowing integrated into their payments app.

alternatives.heading: Klover Cash Advances and Survey Points System
alternatives.body:
Klover provides cash advances ranging from $25 to $750, with an average advance of approximately $170. Klover charges no interest, no late fees and no credit check. Its cash advance page and official FAQ confirm advance limits of up to $750. Standard delivery is free and takes between 2 and 5 business days. Users who need instant access can pay an optional express transfer fee.

Klover generates revenue through these express delivery fees and optional Klover+ paid memberships. The app includes a points system where users can complete surveys and watch advertisements to increase their advance limit or offset charges. Klover also includes basic budgeting tools and optional credit score tracking.

Analyzing the cost of a $100 advance shows the difference in optional costs. Dave requires an overdraft fee of $5 (the greater of $5 or 5%) plus up to $5 for the monthly membership fee, totaling $10 before any external debit transfer fee. Klover charges $0 in monthly subscription fees for its basic tier. If a user selects standard delivery on Klover, the $100 advance costs $0, provided the user can wait 2 to 5 business days. Choosing an express transfer adds a fee, but avoids Dave's recurring monthly charge.

Klover standard delivery takes 2 to 5 business days, whereas Dave ExtraCash is typically authorized within 5 minutes and transfers to Dave Checking at no added cost. Klover fits individuals who want small advances without subscription fees and are willing to engage with surveys to boost limits.

alternatives.heading: Albert Instant Advance and Premium Subscription Tiers
alternatives.body:
Albert is a financial technology company that partners with Stride Bank, N.A. for Albert Cash and Wells Fargo, N.A. for savings accounts, providing pass-through FDIC insurance up to $250,000 under qualifying conditions. Albert offers Instant Advances from $25 to $1,000 with no interest, no late fees and no credit check, though Albert states that few customers qualify for the full $1,000. Albert does not require a paid subscription to access an Instant Advance. For other credit products, Albert provides an Instant Line of Credit through FinWise Bank with draw fees, and an Instant Loan starting at $1,000 that involves a soft credit pull.

Albert offers optional paid subscription tiers ranging from $19.99 to $39.99 per month, following a 30-day trial. Subscribers gain access to automated savings, budgeting tools, virtual cards with custom spending limits, and high-yield savings earning 3.50% APY (variable, current as of November 19, 2026). Cash balances held without an eligible paid subscription do not receive this yield.

Comparing recurring costs between Dave and Albert shows a wide gap in subscription pricing. Dave charges up to $5 per month, totaling up to $60 annually ($5 x 12). Albert's paid tiers cost $19.99 per month ($239.88 per year) on the lower tier and $39.99 per month ($479.88 per year) on the upper tier. However, for a user who strictly uses Albert for an Instant Advance with standard delivery and declines the subscription, the annual subscription cost is $0. On savings, a $1,000 balance earning 3.50% APY on Albert generates $35.00 in annual interest, which partially offsets subscription costs if the user maintains paid features.

Albert has higher recurring subscription costs than Dave if the user enrolls in a paid plan, as Albert's monthly fee ranges from $19.99 to $39.99 compared to Dave's $5 cap. Albert fits consumers who want access to advances up to $1,000 without a mandatory subscription, or who want premium automated financial planning tools.

alternatives.heading: Who This Is Not For
alternatives.body:
- Borrowers who need long-term financing or large sums: cash advance apps provide short-term liquidity under $1,500. They do not replace personal installment loans or credit lines for major expenses.
- Individuals without regular income: services such as MoneyLion, Varo and Cash App require qualifying deposits or income to access advances.
- Residents of excluded states: Cash App Borrow is explicitly unavailable in Colorado, Iowa and Oregon.

alternatives.heading: What Would Change Our Answer
alternatives.body:
- Dave eliminating its up-to-$5 monthly membership fee, which would lower the baseline cost for occasional borrowers.
- MoneyLion adjusting its 7.5% and 9% Turbo delivery rates or removing the $100 disbursement cap.
- Varo altering its flat fee scale that currently charges between $1.60 and $100 per advance.
- EarnIn introducing mandatory monthly fees or altering its $1,500 Live Pay limit.

stillBetterFit.heading: When Dave Is Still the Better Fit
stillBetterFit.body:
Dave remains an effective choice for individuals who want an integrated digital checking account with built-in overdraft advance capability. ExtraCash allows advances up to $500 without a credit check, late fees or interest charges. Because Dave uses CashAI to evaluate 180 or more data points, gig workers and freelancers with irregular earnings can qualify based on spending patterns, income and bank balances.

 Dave requires no minimum deposit (allowing users to open the account with as little as $1), no minimum balance, and no minimum-balance or account closing fees. Account holders receive a digital Dave Debit Mastercard compatible with Apple Pay and Google Pay, with physical cards mailed by the United States Postal Service (USPS) within 10 business days. Cardholders access 40,000 or more fee-free ATMs through the MoneyPass network, and can deposit cash at Walgreens and 90,000 other retail locations via Green Dot for a service fee up to $4.95. Direct deposits can arrive up to 2 days early depending on payer timing.

Transferring an ExtraCash advance directly into Dave Checking incurs no transfer fee. A member who pays the $5 monthly membership and takes a $100 advance pays $5 for the overdraft fee and $0 for delivery. For existing Dave Checking users who value integrated Round Up savings, budgeting features and cash advances inside one application, Dave puts those tools in one app.

verdict:
Dave combines banking, budgeting and cash advances up to $500, but its up-to-$5 monthly membership fee and 5% overdraft charges create recurring costs. MoneyLion and EarnIn offer pathways to larger advances without mandatory monthly subscriptions, while Varo provides a full chartered bank experience with high-yield savings. Cash App, Klover and Albert serve different niches across peer-to-peer payments, task-based limit increases and automated budgeting.

Pick a Dave alternative to check first by writing down the advance amount you need, then add each app's delivery fee for that amount from the table and see more fee breakdowns in the [comparison hub](/compare/).

faqs.question: Is Dave a bank?
faqs.answer: Dave is a financial technology company, not a bank. Deposit accounts and banking services are provided by Coastal Community Bank, Member FDIC, or another partner bank, with deposits insured up to $250,000 on a pass-through basis.

faqs.question: How much does Dave cost per month?
faqs.answer: Dave charges a monthly membership fee of up to $5. This fee renews automatically every month to maintain access to ExtraCash, Income Opportunity Services and Financial Management Services, even if the user deletes the app.

faqs.question: What is the Dave ExtraCash overdraft fee?
faqs.answer: ExtraCash is structured as an overdraft and carries an overdraft fee equal to the greater of $5 or 5% of the advance amount. A $100 advance incurs a $5 fee, while a $500 advance incurs a $25 fee.

faqs.question: Is there a cash advance app with no monthly fee?
faqs.answer: MoneyLion Instacash, EarnIn and Klover provide cash advances without mandatory monthly membership fees. Albert also allows Instant Advances without requiring enrollment in its paid subscription tiers.

faqs.question: Which Dave alternative offers the largest advance?
faqs.answer: EarnIn offers access to up to $1,500 per pay period through Live Pay based on hours worked. MoneyLion, Varo and Albert each provide advance limits up to $1,000 subject to account qualification.
